paper_title: Hard Sample-Conditioned Decorrelated Attention for Robust Face Recognition

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles. Correlation-based penalties encourage head disentanglement, yet apply uniform regularization across all training samples. In face recognition (FR), hard samples whose embeddings lie close to competing identities are critical for optimization and generalization. Motivated by this, we propose ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty: samples with high cosine similarity to negative class centers receive stronger head decorrelation, enforcing specialization where identity ambiguity is highest. Experiments show improvements over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Our analysis shows that ViT-HarDis reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing inter-head attention similarity, and that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing the entire network. Trained on WebFace4M, ViT-HarDis achieves SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1, while achieving the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, improving FR without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. Code: https://github.com/TaharChettaoui/Hard-Sample-Conditioned-Attention-for-FR.

sections.content: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles. Correlation-based penalties encourage head disentanglement, yet apply uniform regularization across all training samples. In face recognition (FR), hard samples whose embeddings lie close to competing identities are critical for optimization and generalization. Motivated by this, we propose ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty: samples with high cosine similarity to negative class centers receive stronger head decorrelation, enforcing specialization where identity ambiguity is highest. Experiments show improvements over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Our analysis shows that ViT-HarDis reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing interhead attention similarity, and that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing the entire network. Trained on WebFace4M, ViTHarDis achieves SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1, while achieving the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, improving FR without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. Code: https://github.com/ TaharChettaoui/Hard-Sample-ConditionedAttention-for-FR. 1. Introduction Face recognition (FR) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, driven by advances in deep neural network architectures, innovations in training objectives, particularly margin-based softmax losses, and the availability of large-scale annotated face datasets [2, 9, 10, 19, 34]. Recent years have witnessed shift from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [15] to Vision Transformers (ViTs) [13], which leverage multi-head attention to capture complex spatial relationships and identity-discriminative patterns. ViT-based FR systems have demonstrated competitive performance on evaluation benchmarks, establishing themselves as promising direction for FR [47, 20, 31]. Although multi-head attention enables ViT to capture diverse representations, prior works [21, 26, 33] in general computer vision have shown that many attention heads become highly correlated or redundant, thus limiting the effective utilization of model capacity. An existing attention head disentanglement method [1], primarily developed for general vision tasks, addresses this issue by uniformly penalizing correlations between attention heads. However, this approach treats all samples equally and does not account for differences in sample difficulty. In practice, hard samples that lie near decision boundaries are more critical for learning and generalization [17, 19, 25]. We argue that attention head specialization should be adaptive, applying stronger disentanglement to these challenging cases, better exploiting model capacity while preserving complementary attention patterns where they are most needed. Motivated by these observations, we propose ViTHarDis, hard sample-conditioned attention head disentanglement framework for ViT-based FR. Instead of uniformly encouraging attention head diversity, our method adaptively strengthens decorrelation according to sample difficulty, promoting specialization for identity-ambiguous samples while preserving the original architecture. Beyond this adaptive regularization strategy, we analyze attention head redundancy in ViT-based FR, revealing that increasing the number of attention heads leads to higher redundancy without improving recognition accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that ViT-HarDis outperforms both the baseline ViT and uniform disentanglement (ViT-Dis) on most considered benchmarks, including IJB-B [35], IJB-C [24], and TinyFace [3], while reducing the similarity of hard samples to competing identity centers and decreasing inter-head attention similarity. We further show that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing all layers, indicating that head specialization is layer-dependent. Finally, we train ViT-HarDis on MS1MV3 [10] and WebFace4M [39], achieving SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1 when trained on WebFace4M, and the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. 2. Related Work 2.1. Vision Transformers for Face Recognition ViTs [13] have recently emerged as competitive alternative to CNNs for FR, owing to their ability to capture longrange spatial dependencies through self-attention. Early studies demonstrated the feasibility of applying ViTs to FR by learning discriminative facial representations from local facial regions. For example, Sun et al. [31] proposed landmark-guided part-based ViT that aggregates local facial patches to improve recognition performance, while ARTriViT [18] introduced Siamese ViT architecture trained with triplet loss for metric learning. Subsequent works focused on improving the robustness and scalability of ViTbased FR models. TransFace [7] proposed dominant patch perturbation and entropy-based hard sample mining to improve optimization and generalization. KP-RPE [20] introduced keypoint-relative positional encoding to enhance robustness against pose and geometric variations by incorporating facial landmark information into the attention mechanism. More recently, FRoundation [4] demonstrated that large pre-trained ViT-based foundation models can be effectively adapted to FR using parameter-efficient finetuning, while SwinFace [28] extended transformer-based facial analysis through multi-task learning framework that jointly performs FR, expression recognition, age estimation, and facial attribute prediction. Chettaoui et al. [5] further improved ViT-based FR by introducing register tokens to better structure attention and reduce attention artifacts. Despite these advances, existing ViT-based FR methods focus on improving network architectures, positional encoding, or training strategies [7, 20], while the behavior of individual attention heads remains largely unexplored. In particular, they do not explicitly encourage heads to learn complementary identity-discriminative features. 2.2. Attention Head Disentanglement Multi-head self-attention enables ViTs to capture complementary information by attending to multiple representation subspaces [13]. Nevertheless, several studies have shown that many attention heads become redundant after training [21, 26, 33]. Voita et al. [33] demonstrated that only small subset of attention heads contributes substantially to model performance, while many remaining heads can be pruned with negligible performance degradation. Similar observations have also been reported for ViT, where heads often exhibit highly correlated attention patterns and unequal contributions to the final prediction [21]. These findings suggest Figure 1. Overview of ViT-HarDis. ViT with blocks and heads encodes batch of face images (1). Per sample, the head-similarity matrix Cb of block ℓ gives the disentanglement loss L(b) Dis (2a), weighted by the sample hardness wb (2b). The weighted penalty LHarDis is summed over the selected blocks and added to the FR loss with weight λ. that multi-head attention capacity is often underutilized. Motivated by these observations, DeCAtt [1] introduces correlation-based regularization that penalizes similarities between attention maps of different heads, encouraging complementary attention patterns without modifying the architecture. DeCAtt was evaluated on general vision tasks rather than FR, and applies the same regularization across all training samples, irrespective of their difficulty. Meanwhile, hard sample learning has become an essential component of modern FR systems. Methods such as CurricularFace [17], MagFace [25] and AdaFace [19] demonstrate that emphasizing hard samples improves discriminative representation learning. Unlike these methods, which incorporate sample difficulty into the optimization objective, our approach leverages sample difficulty to adaptively guide attention head disentanglement. By enforcing stronger attention decorrelation particularly for identityambiguous samples, our method encourages more effective attention head specialization while preserving the original ViT architecture [13]. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to condition attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty for ViT-based FR. 3. Methodology This section presents ViT-HarDis, our hard sampleconditioned approach to attention head disentanglement for ViT-based FR, illustrated in Figure 1. Attention head decorrelation reduces redundancy between heads, but applies uniform penalty across all samples, independent of how difficult each is to recognize. ViT-HarDis instead conditions this penalty on sample difficulty, quantified by the proximity of samples embedding to competing class centers, so that heads specialize where identity ambiguity is highest. We first provide preliminaries on ViT and attention head disentanglement, followed by our proposed ViT-HarDis. 3.1. Hard Sample-Conditioned Disentanglement While existing attention disentanglement methods [1] apply uniform disentanglement across all training samples, hard samples are known to contribute disproportionately to FR optimization and to require dedicated mining or weighting strategies [17, 19, 29]. Motivated by this, we condition attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty, encouraging head specialization on hard samples (Section 5.2). Let eb denote the normalized embedding of sample b, yb its true class label, wc the normalized center of class c, and sb,c = eb, wc the cosine similarity of sample to center c. We categorize samples by whether the true class center is the closest. Wrong samples are misclassified i.e., maxc=yb sb,c > sb,yb . Among the correctly classified samples, easy samples lie far from any negative center, whereas hard samples have high similarity to the closest negative center, creating embedding ambiguity that requires stronger specialization to resolve. We propose to condition attention head disentanglement on sample hardness, assigning stronger disentanglement to hard samples according to their similarity to the closest negative identity (i.e., the wrong identity with the highest similarity). For sample b, we define its hardness as the maximum cosine similarity to negative class center: hb = max c=yb sb,c. (8) The maximum is computed over all negative class centers wc. Wrong samples are excluded from the weighting to avoid amplifying potential label noise or annotation errors in the training data. We therefore map the hardness to [0, 1] and set the weight of wrong samples to zero: hb = hb + 1 2 , 0, if sb,yb > maxc=yb sb,c otherwise (wrong samples) (9) The per-sample weight is obtained by normalizing hb by its batch mean, and weights the per-sample disentanglement penalty L(b) Dis (Section 3.2): wb = hb 1 (cid:80)B b= hb + ϵ , LHarDis = 1 (cid:88) b= wb L(b) Dis, (10) where ϵ is small constant for numerical stability. The weight wb is computed from the current embeddings and class centers, but is detached and treated as constant. No gradient is propagated through wb into eb or wc, so the hardness estimate acts as per-sample scaling factor. Gradients from LHarDis reach the backbone only through the attention maps. Since wb has (approximately) unit mean over the batch, the weighting does not rescale the overall penalty but redistributes it toward harder samples. Because the weights may correlate with the per-sample penalty, the realized penalty of ViT-HarDis can still differ from that of ViT-Dis. This loss is combined with margin-penalty-based objective [2, 9, 19, 34] to form the total training loss: Ltotal = LFR + λLHarDis, (11) where λ is the disentanglement weight factor and LFR is the margin-penalty based loss. This formulation encourages each attention head to specialize in distinct patterns by penalizing overlap between the attention maps of different heads, while the FR loss drives the model to learn discriminative identity embeddings [2, 9, 19, 34]. The disentanglement penalty can be applied at any of the transformer In our case, LHarDis is summed over the selected blocks. blocks. An ablation on which blocks to apply the disentanglement to is presented in Section 5.3. 4. Experimental Setup Training Datasets: We train our ViT models on MS1MV3 [10] and WebFace4M [39], two datasets widely used in FR research. MS1MV3 is cleaned iteration of MS-Celeb1M [14], containing 5.2M images of 93K identities, while WebFace4M is subset of WebFace260M [39] with 4M images of 200K identities. All images are aligned and resized to 112112 using five facial landmarks predicted by RetinaFace [11], following [20]. For ablation studies, we use subset of MS1MV3 containing 10K randomly selected identities and approximately 600K images, denoted MS1MV310K. This subset keeps the ablation studies computationally tractable, while the SOTA comparison in Section 5.5 uses the full datasets. Evaluation Datasets: We evaluate our models on LFW [16], CFP-FP [30], AgeDB30 [27], CA-LFW [37], and CPLFW [36], reporting verification accuracies (%) following the official protocol of each benchmark. We further evaluate on the large-scale IJB-B [35] and IJB-C [24] benchmarks using the official 1:1 mixed verification protocol, reporting true acceptance rates (TAR) at false acceptance rates (FAR) of 104 and 105. These benchmarks are commonly used to evaluate recent advances in FR and cover diverse range of use cases [2, 7, 12, 34]. Finally, we evaluate on TinyFace [3], which consists of unconstrained low-resolution face images, to assess robustness beyond controlled scenarios. Model Architecture: As our base model, we employ ViT with KeyPoint Relative Position Encoding (KP-RPE) [20], which leverages keypoints (e.g., facial landmarks) to make ViT more resilient to scale, translation, and pose variations, making it strong ViT-based FR baseline. We explore two ViT-KP-RPE backbones: ViT-S (Small) and ViTB (Base), with all models using an input image size of 112 112 and patch size of 8. ViT-S is used for ablation studies and has 12 transformer layers. We study the effect of different numbers of attention heads (4, 8, 16, and 32) in Section 5.1, and adopt 16 heads for the remaining ablations. We apply set of data augmentation techniques, following [20]. 5. Results In this section, we validate ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty. We first investigate redundancy in multi-head attention by analyzing how the number of heads affects FR performance and inter-head similarity (Section 5.1), finding that additional heads introduce redundancy without improving performance. Section 5.2 then demonstrates the benefits of hard sample-conditioned disentanglement over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement. In Section 5.3, we study the layer selection strategy, finding that disentangling only the final layers outperforms full-network application. Section 5.4 ablates the disentanglement weight λ, and Section 5.5 compares ViT-HarDis against SOTA methods. In this section, we investigate how the number of attention heads affects FR performance in ViT-KP-RPE. Accordingly, we evaluate four configurations (4, 8, 16, and 32 heads), with verification accuracy results presented in Table 1, and analyze the resulting attention patterns across depths in Figure 2. We make the following observations: From Table 1, which reports verification accuracy across the considered configurations on several evaluation benchmarks defined in Section 4, we observe that verification performance is largely stable across configurations. The model with the fewest attention heads achieves the best results on both large-scale benchmarks, IJB-B and IJB-C, but the differences are small and the ranking varies on other benchmarks. Overall, additional attention heads yield no consistent gain, indicating that the number of heads has limited impact on verification performance. From Figure 2, which presents the maximum inter-head attention cosine similarity across transformer depths for the considered configurations, we observe that as the number of attention heads increases, inter-head cosine similarity rises across most depths. This suggests that additional heads do not develop specialized roles, but instead learn redundant attention patterns. Together, the minimal performance variance in Table 1 and the high inter-head redundancy in Figure 2 indicate that additional heads are not effectively used. This motivates head disentanglement to enforce meaningful specialization. For all remaining ablations in Sections 5.25.4, we adopt ViT-S with 16 attention heads, matching the head count of the ViT-B backbone used in our SOTA comparison and exhibiting clear inter-head redundancy. 5.2. Hard Sample-conditioned Disentanglement In this section, we validate that the model trained with hard sample-conditioned disentanglement (ViT-HarDis) outperforms both baseline (ViT) and uniform disentanglement (ViT-Dis) on most considered benchmarks. For ViT-Dis and ViT-HarDis, we apply the disentanglement to the final transformer blocks (1012), which yields the best results as shown in Section 5.3. We set λ = 1 for both, and study its effect in Section 5.4, which confirms λ = 1 as the bestperforming value on the large-scale benchmarks. Face verification performance. This shows that excluding wrong samples further improves performance on most benchmarks, consistent with avoiding the amplification of potential label noise. Influence on hard samples. To assess hard sample ambiguity, we first compute the cosine similarity of all training samples in MS1MV310K to their closest negative class center using the baseline ViT-KP-RPE Small, then select the 10% hardest samples. Figure 3 shows their similarity distribution for all three variants. We observe that the mean cosine similarity of hard samples to their closest negative class center is 0.40 for the baseline, dropping to 0.35 for uniform disentanglement, and reaching 0.31 for ViT-HarDis. This demonstrates that our approach reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers, thereby lowering embedding ambiguity and improving identity discrimination. We further track the fraction of wrong samples, as defined in Section 3.3, throughout training. Figure 4 shows that it starts near 100% at initialization, when class centers are untrained, and decreases sharply during training. On MS1MV310K, about 16% of samples remain excluded after ten epochs, dropping to roughly 2% by the end. MS1MV3 converges fastest, falling to about 2% within ten epochs, while WebFace4M converges more slowly but reaches the lowest final fraction at about 0.4%. Attention maps analysis. Figure 5 visualizes the average attention maps across hard samples (top 10% from MS1MV310K) for all 16 attention heads in the three variants. The baseline and ViT-Dis exhibit substantial redundancy, with most heads concentrating on similar facial regions (e.g., both eyes), whereas ViT-HarDis shows reduced redundancy, with individual heads specializing on distinct regions. This is quantified by the average inter-head attention similarity across all hard samples: 0.21 for the baseline, 0.09 for ViT-Dis, and 0.01 for ViT-HarDis. This reduction indicates that hard sample-conditioned disentanglement enforces head specialization, with each head focusing on complementary facial features rather than redundantly attending to the same regions, which contributes to improved identity discrimination on hard samples, as shown in Figure 3. Computational cost. Our approach does not modify the ViT-KP-RPE backbone and introduces no additional parameters or operations at inference. Inference cost is therefore identical to the baseline, and only training time is affected. All models were trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 SXM4 40 GB GPUs, using the parameters defined in Section 4. Layer Selection for Attention Disentanglement In this section, we investigate the optimal layer selection strategy for hard sample-conditioned attention disentanglement in ViT-KP-RPE Small. Accordingly, we evaluate two layer selection approaches with varying coverage (25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of layers). From the verification accuracy results on several evaluation benchmarks presented in Table 3, we make the following observations: Disentangling only the final layers (1012, 25% of total layers) achieves the best average performance and the best results on the large-scale benchmarks, yielding 85.72% on IJB-B and 89.09% on IJB-C, against 82.20% and 83.94% for full disentanglement. For both selection strategies, the 25% coverage variant achieves the best average and large-scale results, with performance degrading as more layers are disentangled. Disentanglement Weight Ablation In this section, we investigate the effect of the disentanglement weight λ on ViT-HarDis, which controls the strength of the hard sample-conditioned disentanglement relative to the FR loss in the total objective, defined in Section 3.3. Accordingly, we evaluate range of values λ {0.5, 1, 1.75, 2.5, 5, 10}. From the verification accuracy results on several evaluation benchmarks presented in Table 4, we observe that λ = 1 gives the best results on the large-scale benchmarks, with 85.72% on IJB-B and 89.09% on IJB-C. While λ = 0.5 gives marginally higher benchmark average, we prioritize the large-scale benchmarks as the more challenging evaluation setting. Performance tends to decrease as λ increases further, with the lowest largescale results at λ = 10 (87.81% on IJB-C), suggesting that very strong disentanglement penalty can come at the expense of the FR objective. We therefore fix λ = 1, which we use as the default value in our other ablation experiments as well as for the SOTA comparison. 5.5. Comparison with SOTA Methods In this section, we compare ViT-HarDis against SOTA ViTbased FR methods trained on MS1MV3 [10] and WebFace4M [39]. While most ViT-based approaches adopt ViTB, their configurations often differ in attention heads, patch size, embedding dimension, or transformer depth, which can influence performance and computational efficiency. To enable compatible comparison to previous methods, we employ ViT-B with 24 transformer layers in the SOTA comparison, unlike the previous ablations which used ViT-KPRPE Small with 12 layers. Following Section 5.3, we apply hard sample-conditioned disentanglement to the final 25% of layers, corresponding to layers 1924. As shown in Table 5, ViT-HarDis trained on WebFace4M achieves the highest results among ViT-based approaches on IJB-B [35] and IJB-C [24], with 95.84% and 97.24%, respectively, as well as the best TinyFace Rank-1 accuracy of 75.97%. When trained on MS1MV3, ViT-HarDis achieves the best IJB-B result (96.14%) and the best TinyFace Rank-1 accuracy (73.52%), while ranking second on IJB-C, closely behind ViT-8R [5]. For fairer comparison, we also retrained KP-RPE [20] under the same training settings as ViT-HarDis, marked with in Table 5. These differ from the published results by at most 0.3 percentage points on the large-scale benchmarks and TinyFace Rank-1. 6. Conclusion We presented ViT-HarDis, hard sample-conditioned attention disentanglement approach. Through comprehensive experiments, ViT-HarDis yielded improvements on most considered benchmarks over the baseline and uniform disentanglement. Additionally, we show that our approach reduces the cosine similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing inter-head attention similarity, enabling individual heads to develop diversified complementary patterns. We further show that disentangling only the final transformer layers outperforms full-network application, indicating that head specialization is layer-dependent. Finally, we train ViT-HarDis on MS1MV3 and WebFace4M, achieving SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank1 when trained on WebFace4M, and the best IJB-B and TinyFace accuracy when trained on MS1MV3. Since the penalty operates only during training, inference cost is unchanged, at the cost of 30% longer training time on WebFace4M. These results validate that sample difficulty effectively guides attention head specialization in FR, improving accuracy without architectural modifications.
